title: CIA Report Warns Israel Could Head Toward Civil War, Total Collapse
author: Aída Chávez
content:

Israel is at risk of civil war or state collapse, a classified CIA assessment
warns, as years of genocide in Gaza and war in Lebanon and Iran deepen
political, economic, and social fractures within the country.

The August report, titled "Fracture From Within," was compiled by experts in
the CIA's Red Cell, according to two U.S. sources who described the contents
of the report to Drop Site News. The Red Cell, which is the unit responsible
for providing "alternative analysis" within the agency, produced the
assessment through a combination of open source information and U.S.
intelligence. The assessment appears to refer only to Israel's Jewish citizens
and does not consider its Palestinian citizens, who make up approximately 20%
of Israel's population and who live under various forms of discrimination that
Amnesty International and other human rights groups have labelled as part of a
broader system of apartheid. The CIA did not respond to a request for comment.

CIA experts pointed to a volatile mix of pressures converging ahead of
Israel's elections on October 27: economic crisis and soaring military
spending; heavily armed veterans returning from prolonged combat, many
carrying serious psychological trauma; growing fury over ultra-Orthodox men
who are exempt from military service; escalating settler violence in the
occupied West Bank; and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fighting to
hold onto power and igniting a constitutional crisis.

The CIA's "red teams" are tasked with developing analysis and ideas that
challenge prevailing assumptions and expose groupthink or blind spots that can
take hold within the intelligence apparatus. "The writers of this are Israel
experts," a source in the intelligence community noted, "this isn't a
fantastical what if--with the upcoming election and the fissures in Israel we
should take seriously their conclusion that Israel is one spark away from real
internal conflict."

One of the deepest fractures in Israeli politics has emerged not over
opposition to the country's war crimes--but over who is expected to fight and
who is exempt. Ultra-Orthodox men have historically received broad exemptions
from military service while continuing to receive state benefits, an
arrangement that has become increasingly contentious amid repeated reserve
mobilizations. Their collective refusal to serve is not rooted in opposition
to Israel's wars, as ultra-Orthodox leaders argue that military service
threatens religious life and their obligation to Torah study. But after years
in which reservists have been repeatedly called away from their jobs and
families, the [exemption](https://apnews.com/article/israel-ultraorthodox-
elections-netanyahu-haredim-military-3f8939b7c601b1dbef16427f422590ed) has
become a potent source of resentment in Israeli society. Households have also
been absorbing the costs of Israel's belligerent policies. Food prices have
reached [record highs](https://www.timesofisrael.com/israelis-hit-by-soaring-
food-prices-as-producers-grocers-feast-on-wartime-windfall/), with the cost of
food--including fresh fruit and vegetables--rising 9.5 percent over the past
two years, deepening an already severe cost-of-living crisis after years of
war.

Yet much of the opposition to Netanyahu is not opposition to Israel's
brutality against Palestinians, but anger over how he has managed it. The
major anti-Netanyahu Zionist parties are themselves divided over leadership
and coalition strategy, while a central line of attack against Netanyahu has
been his responsibility for the October 7 security failure. Recent
[polling](https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/elections/2026-09-24/ty-
article/.premium/channel-13-news-poll-eisenkot-bloc-leads-with-52-seats-
netanyahu-bloc-with-51/000001a0-cfc1-decb-affc-dfe9ca2f0000) has shown both
the Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs struggling to reach the 61 seats
required to govern.

The sources warned that the combination of political fracture and a growing
population of heavily armed, traumatized veterans has historical precedents.
"Famously the Freikorps of Germany were PTSD-addled veterans with weapons and
bloodthirst," he said. "I'm not saying Israel post Gaza is Germany post-WWI
but there are certainly aspects of this that ring similar to me."

Israel is also confronting growing isolation abroad, including an erosion of
support in the United States that Israeli officials themselves have privately
treated as a long-term threat. The August report pointed to Israel
increasingly becoming a pariah state as a factor that could lead to state
breakdown.

According to another CIA assessment Capital & Empire
[reported](https://capitalandempire.com/p/exclusive-cia-assessment-israel-us-
support) in July, Israeli officials believe the American political consensus
underpinning the alliance is breaking down and that continued reliance on
billions of dollars in direct U.S. military aid may eventually become
politically untenable. Their response has been to seek deeper integration into
the American military, intelligence, and defense establishment--ties that
would be harder for future governments to unwind. By this spring, 60% of
Americans viewed Israel unfavorably, up from 53% a year earlier, according to
a Pew Research Center [survey](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-
reads/2026/04/07/negative-views-of-israel-netanyahu-continue-to-rise-among-
americans-especially-young-people/).

That deterioration of support is increasingly visible inside the U.S. national
security establishment, as well. "The intelligence community, like America,
like the military, like everywhere, is growing frustrated with the real and
political capital that's spent on propping up Israel," the source said. "As
we're moving forward with further integrating our military-industrial capacity
with them, there's deep frustration that we're doing this for a country that
dragged us into a war we're losing, a country that spies on us."

The CIA report also tried to game out how these pressures could interact if
Israel's internal crisis deepened--how a single spark could turn political
fracture into open civil conflict, and what would follow from there. Among the
scenarios raised were foreign technology and artificial-intelligence companies
pulling investment or personnel from Israel, further eroding an already
strained economy, regional governments reconsidering the political and
strategic value of deeper normalizing relations with Israel, and Hamas or
Hezbollah exploiting a period of domestic weakness. The report specifically
used the term "civil conflict," according to the sources.

For decades, Israel's power depended not only on weapons and American backing,
but on the projection that its military dominance, intelligence superiority,
and internal cohesion made the state effectively unbreakable. But as the
assessment warned, beneath that projection of overwhelming force, Israel is
accumulating economic, political, and social contradictions that military
might alone may not be able to contain.
